findings.claim: Today there are approximately 430,000 Sikhs living in Britain, with large communities in Southall (west London), Birmingham, Leicester and Bradford.
findings.truth: 430,000 is close to the 2011 figure. The 2021 census counted 524,140 Sikhs in England and Wales; Scotland's 2022 census counted 10,988, so Britain holds more than 530,000. The largest local Sikh populations are Sandwell (39,252), Birmingham (33,126), Wolverhampton (31,769), Ealing (28,491) and Hillingdon (26,339). Leicester and Bradford are not among them.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Sikhism in the United Kingdom (2021 census, England and Wales; 2022 census, Scotland)

findings.claim: It contains the hymns of the ten human Gurus and other saints.
findings.truth: Only six of the ten Gurus have compositions in the Guru Granth Sahib: Nanak, Angad, Amar Das, Ram Das, Arjan and Tegh Bahadur. Guru Hargobind, Guru Har Rai and Guru Har Krishan added none, and Guru Gobind Singh's own poetry is not in it. The rest is by thirteen Hindu bhagats, two Muslim saint poets, bhatts and Gursikhs.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Guru Granth Sahib (hymn counts by Guru)

findings.claim: containing the hymns of the ten human Gurus
findings.truth: Same error as F2 in the glossary definition of Guru Granth Sahib.

findings.claim: 'State two attributes of God as expressed in the Mool Mantra.' labelled '2 marks - State / Give'
findings.truth: This paper sets no 2-mark question. Each religion carries two five-part questions of 1, 1, 4, 6 and 12 marks, and the second short part is worth 1 mark for one item. Rewritten as a 1-mark, one-item question.
findings.evidence: spec 3.1.7 assessment pages: 'two five-part questions of 1, 1, 4, 6 and 12 marks'; section 4.4.1

findings.claim: without naming the Mool Mantra and at least one attribute from it (e.g. Ik Onkar, Karta Purakh), your response cannot reach the top band
findings.truth: The 6-mark question asks for a sacred writing or another source of religious belief and teaching. Any relevant Sikh source qualifies, so a top-band answer need not name the Mool Mantra specifically. The invented constraint would mislead a student who cited another Guru Granth Sahib teaching.
findings.evidence: spec section 4, assessment objectives: 'key sources of wisdom and authority including scripture and/or sacred texts'

findings.claim: illusion (maya), lust (kam), anger (krodh), greed (lobh), worldly attachment (moh) and pride (ahankar). These are sometimes described as the five vices (panj dosh).
findings.truth: Six items are listed and then called the five vices. The five vices, or five thieves (panj chor), are kam, krodh, lobh, moh and ahankar. Maya is a separate barrier, and 'panj dosh' is not the standard term.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Five Thieves; spec 3.1.7.1 lists illusion separately from the five

findings.claim: 'Give two of the five stages of liberation (khands)' labelled '2 marks - State / Give'
findings.truth: No 2-mark question exists on this paper. Rewritten as a 1-mark, one-item question.

findings.claim: Saying 'the Guru Granth Sahib teaches...' followed by a developed point will take you into the top band.
findings.truth: The 6-mark question asks for two reasons. One developed point cannot reach the top band.
findings.evidence: spec section 4.4.1 question structure; the question's own wording ('Explain two reasons')

findings.claim: 'What names did Guru Gobind Singh give to Sikh men and Sikh women' labelled '2 marks - State / Give'
findings.truth: No 2-mark question exists on this paper, and the short part asks for one item. Rewritten as a 1-mark question on the name Kaur.

findings.claim: A Mastering answer names the sub-traditions (sahajdhari and amritdhari) and reaches a justified conclusion.
findings.truth: There is no such requirement. The spec offers sahajdhari and amritdhari only as an example of Sikh perspectives students may refer to, and they are not needed for a top-band answer on equality.
findings.evidence: spec 3.1.7 preamble: 'Students may refer to a range of Sikh perspectives ... for example ...'

findings.claim: The Guru Granth Sahib describes the sangat using the image of iron sharpening iron
findings.truth: 'As iron sharpens iron, so one person sharpens another' is Proverbs 27:17 from the Hebrew Bible. It is not a Guru Granth Sahib image. Attributing a Biblical proverb to Sikh scripture in five places, including a flashcard that asks the student to recall it, would cost marks and could offend. Replaced with the plain Sikh teaching that the company a person keeps shapes them, with no invented quotation.
findings.evidence: Proverbs 27:17 (NIV) via Bible Gateway; no such image found in Sikh sources checked

findings.claim: 'State two types of sewa in Sikh teaching.' labelled '2 marks - State / Give'
findings.truth: No 2-mark question exists on this paper. Rewritten as a 1-mark, one-item question.

findings.claim: This counts as a named source of religious teaching and takes your answer into the top band.
findings.truth: Naming a source is necessary but not sufficient. The 6-mark question needs two reasons, each developed.

findings.claim: Repeated across the unit: 'The mark scheme requires...', 'The mark scheme rewards students who...' (L2 n19/n20, L3 n17, L4 n16).
findings.truth: These claims are about a document we do not cite and cannot show. The substance is defensible in each case, so the options are: leave them; or change the house wording fleet-wide to 'the question tells you to' and 'a strong answer explains that', which says the same thing without asserting what a board mark scheme contains. Recommend the fleet-wide wording change, done as one sweep rather than in this unit alone.
findings.ruling: Leave: fleet-wide mark-scheme wording sweep (relabel queue).

findings.truth: Ajooni and Saibhang are two attributes: beyond birth (not incarnated) and self-existent. Glossing the pair as 'self-existent' alone drops 'beyond birth'. Incomplete rather than wrong, so no edit.
findings.evidence: standard Mool Mantra transliteration and translation

findings.claim: sociological research including studies by the Sikh Network UK
findings.truth: The organisation is The Sikh Network, whose UK Sikh Survey reported caste discrimination among British Sikhs. The substance holds; only the name is loose. Not worth an edit.
findings.evidence: unverified in this session (WebSearch budget spent); claim is plausible and not mark-affecting

findings.claim: 'Any two of: wisdom, truthful living, justice, temperance, self-control, patience, courage, humility, contentment.' and 'Five: Dharam Khand, Gyan Khand, Saram Khand, Karam Khand, Sach Khand.'
findings.truth: Both are comma-list answers, the pattern the flashcard validator discourages. Pre-existing and factually correct, so left alone; flag for the flashcard quality queue.

findings.claim: Sixteenth-century Punjab was a society stratified by caste, religious division and gender inequality.
findings.truth: Guru Nanak's declaration at the River Bein is dated about 1499, the very end of the fifteenth century, though his ministry ran to 1539. The label is loose, not wrong.

summary: Four lessons, all with findings. The serious one is lesson 4: 'iron sharpens iron' (Proverbs 27:17) is attributed to the Guru Granth Sahib in five places, including a flashcard that drills it. The rest are exam-form errors - every lesson carries a 2-mark practice question, a form this paper does not set - plus four invented top-band claims, an out-of-date Sikh population figure, the claim that all ten Gurus wrote in the Guru Granth Sahib, and six barriers labelled as the five vices.
